This topic adds the negatives, which are what make every subtraction have an answer. La letra $\\mathbb{Z}$ se dice <strong>«:
The letter $\mathbb{Z}$ is said “Z” and names the integers: the naturals plus their negatives. It was chosen for Zahl, which in German means “number”.

It reads: “Z is the set made up of, and so on backwards, minus three, minus two, minus one, zero, one, two, three, and so on”.

Notice that the dots are on both sides: unlike the naturals, here there is no beginning and no end.
La regla de los signos se enuncia en una: The rule of signs is stated in one line and believed out of habit, but it has a reasonable explanation. Multiplying by a negative is “the opposite of”: if owing 3 euros five times is $-15$, then no longer owing 3 euros five times has to be $+15$. Minus times minus gives plus because the opposite of the opposite is where you started.
Los negativos aparecen en cuanto hay un: Negatives turn up as soon as there is an agreed zero: temperatures below zero, basement floors, an overdrawn balance, altitudes below sea level, the time difference from Greenwich. The absolute value is what answers “how far off am I?” regardless of direction: a thermostat that has to hold 21 °C does not act on the difference but on its absolute value, because three degrees over and three degrees under are the same deviation.
Los negativos costaron muchísimo de acep: The negatives took an enormous amount of accepting. The Greeks rejected them (“there is nothing less than nothing”); Chinese mathematicians were already using them in the second century with red and black rods for accounting; in India, Brahmagupta (seventh century) was the first to give complete rules of calculation, talking about fortunes and debts. In Europe they were called “absurd numbers” well into the seventeenth century.
Los negativos van a la izquierda del cer: The negatives go to the left of zero; the larger their absolute value, the further left.
